headline: Fact Check: Did Trump clash with a reporter over the six-month Iran war?
trending_context: InfoGram's September 27 X post circulated the fabricated dialogue as a real confrontation; GoGoSpoiler published its fact check on September 28 documenting the clip's 'Satire' label and the account's satire bio. Note: the X post itself could not be opened directly (X blocked), so the label/bio evidence is documented via the fact-check investigations, and no major fact-checker has yet covered this specific video.
trending_claim: A viral video purports to show Trump in a heated exchange with a reporter over the six-month US-Iran war: the journalist says 'You have been at war with Iran for six months now,' Trump answers 'Well, we were in Vietnam for 21 years,' then calls the journalist a 'fake reporter' and orders them out. (X post by InfoGram @_InfoGram_, September 27, 2026.)
rating_explained: This confrontation never happened, and the evidence is affirmative rather than a mere absence of confirmation. The clip is constructed from a motionless still photograph of Trump standing at a podium, and it carries a visible 'Satire' label — the video declares its own fictionality. The originating account, InfoGram, labels its content 'satire commentary' in its X biography and has a documented history of manufacturing fabricated Trump political exchanges for engagement, including a companion fake claiming former CIA Director David Petraeus called Trump a 'liar' over the Iran war. No White House briefing transcript, wire-service report, or verified audio-visual recording contains the 'Vietnam' or 'fake reporter' dialogue. Genuine Trump–reporter exchanges on the Iran war — such as his real 'What a stupid question that is' reply to a nuclear-strike question, documented by established outlets — show what real ones look like; this one exists only as labeled satire. Presenting it as a real event is false.

sources.name: GoGoSpoiler, 'Fact Check: Did former CIA director call Trump a 'liar' over his claims about Iran war?'
InShorts (via Moneycontrol), 'What a stupid question: Trump after reporter asks about nuclear strike on Iran'

headline: Fact check: Trump lies again that grocery prices 'have come way down' this term
trending_context: Trump made the remarks to reporters on September 27; CNN's fact check landed September 28 with a full CPI breakdown. It continues a months-long pattern of Trump claiming broad deflation during this presidency, amid poor inflation polling as the midterms approach.
trending_claim: Trump told reporters on Sunday, September 27: 'The prices for groceries have come way down from Biden. Almost every price has come way down,' adding 'With the exception of oil, everything is going down.'
rating_explained: Federal Consumer Price Index data directly contradicts the claim. Grocery prices (food at home) are up 3.4% on average since January 2025, the month Trump took over from Biden, through August 2026 — not 'way down' — while overall consumer prices are up 4.8% over the same period. Five of the six CPI grocery categories are up substantially: cereals and bakery products (+3.3%), meats, poultry, fish and eggs (+3%), fruits and vegetables (+4.6%), nonalcoholic beverages (+6.3%), and other food at home (+3%); only dairy is roughly flat. Trump has repeatedly touted eggs, which are down 31.1% after an avian-flu spike at the end of Biden's term, but eggs are an outlier — no other product or category has fallen even a third as much. Coffee is up 21.8% and beef and veal up 16.5%. His companion claims fail too: year-over-year inflation was 3% in January 2025 and 3.4% in both July and August 2026 — higher now than what he inherited, not lower — and with a historical peak of 23.7%, he did not inherit 'the worst inflation in the history of our country.' Independent BLS-based reporting from Morningstar and the Providence Journal confirms the 3.4% annual CPI rate and rising food, energy, shelter, and vehicle costs.

sources.name: Morningstar, 'August CPI Report Shows Inflation at a 3.4% Annual Rate, Above Forecasts'
The Providence Journal, 'Inflation increased in August. How much more you may be paying for eggs, gasoline'

headline: Fact Check: Did Trump say Americans will not be able to eat if Democrats win in 2026 midterms?
trending_context: Hakimian's September 29 X post framed three-month-old remarks as breaking news and gathered 5,000+ views within minutes; MEAWW and GoGoSpoiler each published same-day fact checks documenting the June 26 origin.
trending_claim: "JUST IN: Trump says you will not be able to eat food anymore if Democrats win in November." (X post by Spencer Hakimian on September 29; 5,000+ views within minutes.)
rating_explained: The 'no food' line is a genuine Trump quote, but the viral post's presentation of it is false in two material ways. First, it is not 'JUST IN': the words come from Trump's June 26, 2026 address to the Faith and Freedom Coalition's Road to Majority conference — three months before the post. Second, the context is entirely different from what the post implies. The official Senate transcript shows Trump was riffing on communism: after calling Democratic-socialist primary winners in New York 'hardcore, godless communists,' he described what he claimed would follow if such ideologies took hold — 'after two or three years, the country is a disaster area... You'll start living in squalor. There will be no food; there will be no housing; there will be no military; there will be no law and order.' He never said a Democratic midterm victory would stop Americans from eating food. The post lifted a three-month-old anti-communism riff and repackaged it as a brand-new threat about November's midterms. Because the attribution is real but the 'when,' 'what,' and 'about whom' are all wrong, the claim as stated is false.

sources.name: U.S. Senate Democrats, 'TRANSCRIPT: President Trump Addresses the Faith and Freedom Coalition Conference, 6.26.26'
GoGoSpoiler, 'Fact Check: Did Trump say Americans will not be able to eat if Democrats win in 2026 midterms?'

headline: Leaked military memo reveals Trump is preparing the US Army for a Cuba invasion
trending_context: Based on CBS News' review of the memo; widely picked up across outlets and September 28 news roundups.
trending_claim: A leaked internal Army Reserve message — which names no country and orders no deployments — shows President Trump is preparing the U.S. Army for an invasion of Cuba.
rating_explained: Dagens' headline asserts that a leaked internal Army memo reveals President Trump is preparing the U.S. Army for a Cuba invasion. The document CBS News reviewed on September 25 is an Army Reserve headquarters message asking subordinate commands for feedback, due September 25, on possible availability of six unit types (military police, medical, engineer, and logistics formations) for U.S. Southern Command within 90-120 days. Every outlet covering the story agrees the document never mentions Cuba, names no troop numbers or destination, specifies no operation, and contains no deployment orders; the Cuba link rests entirely on unnamed U.S. officials who told CBS the request is tied to continued Cuba planning. On September 26, Trump himself told White House reporters he did not believe the U.S. military would be needed and that 'Cuba and us will make a deal,' and a Southern Command spokesperson declined to confirm specifics, citing operational security. Because the memo itself names no country and issues no orders, the claim that it 'reveals' invasion preparation is not what the document shows: the verified core is a readiness inquiry for Southern Command, while the 'invasion' framing is an inference from anonymous officials. The story mixes real reporting with unsupported framing, so it is misleading rather than accurate — but not false, since CBS's anonymously sourced account of Cuba-directed contingency planning has not been contradicted.

sources.name: Times News NG (verbatim reprint of the original CBS News article 'Army Reserve Weighs Support Units as Trump Says Cuba Deal Likely')
LiveMint — 'US Army plans for possible Cuba operation' (independent outlet, corroborating memo contents and caveats)
Unbiased Headlines — 'Army Reserve Weighs Sending Police and Medical Units Toward Cuba' (corroborates memo details, Southern Command statement, Trump/Rubio/Cuban official remarks)

headline: Fact Check: Is Trump banning federal loans for students in low-earning college majors?
trending_context: The New Republic's September 28 X post promoting its July/August article 'Trump Moves to Cut Off Student Loans for Tons of Degrees' drew more than 20 million views; FactPost's September 28 list post (social work, teaching aides, cosmetology, culinary arts, music, art, English literature, film, religious studies) and other users amplified it. The U.S. Department of Education responded on X the same day calling it 'fake news,' fueling a second wave of debate.
trending_claim: Trump is banning students majoring in degrees that don't make enough money from taking out college loans; degrees for social work, art, religious studies, teaching aides, and music will be hit the hardest. (The New Republic's September 28 X post, 20M+ views, amplified by FactPost and others.)
rating_explained: The viral 'ban' framing materially misstates how the policy works, but it is built on a real rule — so 'false' would overstate the case the other way. The Education Department finalized an earnings-accountability rule (the 'Do No Harm' test, implementing provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act): undergraduate programs whose graduates' median earnings fall below those of typical high-school-diploma holders aged 25–34 — measured via IRS data four years after graduation — in two of three consecutive years lose access to federal Direct Loans; graduate programs face a higher benchmark against bachelor's-degree holders. The earliest penalties land in the 2028–29 academic year, and no program or major is 'banned' — students may still enroll, and the federal government does not set curricula, as the Education Department stressed in its September 28 X post calling the claim 'fake news.' Yet the functional consequence the viral posts point to is real: Inside Higher Ed and The Source confirm programs that fail the test do lose federal Direct Loan eligibility, which can put affected degrees out of reach for students who depend on federal borrowing. 'Trump is banning students' turns a program-level accountability mechanism into a student-level ban, which is why the honest rating is misleading rather than outright false.

sources.name: The Source, 'Thank Trump: In 2027 "If Your Degree Doesn't Make Enough Money" You Won't Get Federal Student Loans'
Inside Higher Ed, 'How Soon Could Colleges Lose Loan Access?'
Feminegra, 'Trump's New College Rule Could Make Social Work and Arts Degrees a Luxury'

headline: Trump admin was ordered to give 30 days notice before releasing citizenship lists. It might not comply
trending_context: Fresh in Google News on September 29.
trending_claim: Judge Paula Xinis ordered the Trump administration to give 30 days' advance notice before activating a federal voter-eligibility portal or providing states citizenship lists, and the administration's objections raise concern it might not comply.
rating_explained: Democracy Docket's own coverage quotes Xinis's order directly: DOJ must 'file a notice with this Court thirty days in advance of any activation of the portal or provision of state citizenship lists,' issued Friday, September 25, 2026 after a hearing. Its related hearing report confirms DOJ attorney Joshua Schopf refused to rule out activating the portal before November 3 and objected to the notice requirement, saying 'If you want to enjoin us, enjoin us.' So the first half of the claim — the 30-day notice order — is factual and verified. But the second half — that the administration 'might not comply' — is speculation, not evidence; vigorous objection to a proposed order is not proof of intent to defy the issued one. Grading the two halves separately: the order is real, the noncompliance claim is inference. The verdict is mixed.

headline: Trump open to Iran sanctions relief for 'concrete progress' on nuclear issues, US official says
trending_context: The Axios report and Trump's Truth Social denial were covered by CNN, Reuters and international outlets September 28–29.
trending_claim: An unnamed U.S. official said Trump was willing to consider Iran sanctions relief as part of a final nuclear deal; Trump responded that he had "offered them NOTHING."
rating_explained: The CNN story asserts a U.S. official told CNN Monday that Trump is willing to give Iran sanctions relief and release frozen funds for "concrete progress" on the nuclear issue, alongside Trump's Truth Social denial, "I offered them NOTHING!" I exhausted the search before rating. The sourcing is structurally thin: Reuters notes "The Axios report did not identify the US officials," and CNN's own piece never names its official. A mandatory second sweep for named officials found none on record supporting the claim: no named U.S. official (Witkoff, Vance, Rubio, or Waltz) has said Trump is willing to offer sanctions relief — UN Ambassador Mike Waltz discussed only the rejected Hormuz proposal. On record against it: Trump himself wrote "This is untrue. I offered them NOTHING" (Reuters), and Iran's FM Abbas Araghchi told IRIB "there has been no change whatsoever in Iran's positions" (CNN). Trump's denial is direct evidence of his stated position, but a public denial cannot disprove private negotiating willingness, and the affirmative sources are unidentified. The core assertion can neither be confirmed nor denied — unverifiable.

headline: Trump DOJ responds to DNC lawsuit, offers no records on ballot seizure plans
trending_context: Widely circulated in election-law and political commentary on September 29.
trending_claim: DOJ's 13-page answer to the DNC's FOIA lawsuit did not deny that the Trump administration considered seizing ballots or voting equipment, identified no responsive records, and offered no timeline for producing them.
rating_explained: The underlying case is real: the DNC filed its complaint on August 20, 2026, docketed as 1:26-cv-02928 in the District of Columbia per the Just Security litigation tracker, and Judge Colleen Kollar-Kotelly ordered DOJ to answer by Monday, September 28, 2026 after rejecting the department's request for an extension. Electionline's Courthouse News reporting confirms the February 2026 FOIA requests and the August lawsuit over records about ballot, machine, or election-material seizures. But the central claim concerns the contents of the 13-page answer itself, and no independent outlet describes those contents — only Democracy Docket's own article, the outlet being fact-checked, characterizes them. Multiple searches for the answer on document repositories and court dockets failed to locate the document, and a direct docket lookup was blocked (403). Because the filing may have occurred as reported yet its contents cannot be independently verified, this story is un verifiable.

headline: Think gas prices are too low? Don't fret, Trump just raised them even higher
trending_context: The fuel-economy rollback led a large Google News cluster on September 29; covered by NYT, NPR, ABC, Detroit Free Press.
trending_claim: NHTSA's own analysis of the CAFE rollback (2031 fleet target cut from 50.4 to 34.9 mpg) projects about $185 billion in added fuel costs and a ~5% rise in CO2 emissions — even as the administration claims the rollback will cut average new-vehicle prices by about $1,300.
rating_explained: Electrek asserts NHTSA's own analysis shows the finalized rollback (2031 fleet target cut from 50.4 to 34.9 mpg) adds $185 billion in fuel costs and ~5% in CO2 emissions, while the administration touts a ~$1,300 per-vehicle price cut. AP reporting confirms DOT/NHTSA finalized the 50.4→34.9 mpg cut for MY2031 and that DOT claims it will reduce the average new-vehicle cost by $1,300 (the final rule's own analysis puts the MY2031 saving at ~$1,290). The $185B/~5% figures are genuine agency numbers: NHTSA's December 2025 Preliminary Regulatory Impact Analysis projected ~100 billion more gallons burned through 2050, roughly $185 billion in added fuel costs, and a near-5% CO2 rise — a Harvard environmental-law review of the NHTSA documents cites the same $185 billion figure. The one imprecision: those exact figures attach to the proposal-stage analysis (34.5 mpg target); the final rule's own 892-page analysis projects a larger fuel increase — a mid-range 122 billion extra gallons through 2050 — so the claim is directionally right and, if anything, conservative. No Snopes/PolitiFact/FactCheck.org/Reuters/AP fact-check rating of this specific claim was found after a dedicated cross-check, and no contradicting evidence emerged, so it rates mostly-accurate rather than fully accurate solely because of the proposal-vs-final attribution.

headline: Oil soars above $107 after Trump rejects Iran peace deal, expects fresh strikes after midterms
trending_context: Covered September 28–29 by WSJ, CNBC, Axios, Bloomberg and Reuters.
trending_claim: The Post reports Trump personally confirmed rejecting Iran's seven-day ceasefire proposal — Hormuz reopened and nuclear talks restarted within a week in exchange for unfrozen Iranian assets, lifted oil sanctions, and an end to the U.S. naval blockade — and, citing the WSJ's anonymous U.S. officials, that he told aides he expects U.S. bombing of Iran to resume after November's midterms; Brent crude topped $107 a barrel and AAA's national gas average hit $4.48/gal.
rating_explained: The Post asserts Trump personally confirmed rejecting Iran's seven-day ceasefire proposal (Hormuz reopened plus nuclear talks in exchange for unfrozen assets, lifted oil sanctions, ended blockade), that he privately told aides he expects U.S. bombing to resume after the November midterms, and that Brent topped $107 with AAA gas at $4.48. The rejection is directly verified: Trump told reporters on camera Saturday 'I reject their proposal' and 'They made a proposal but I rejected it,' as quoted by Open Chronicle and MarketForces Africa, and the proposal terms match Foreign Minister Araghchi's own UNGA statements that Iran would reopen the strait if Washington released frozen funds, waived oil sanctions, and lifted the blockade. Market data verifies the price half: Brent traded to $107.02–$107.26 intraday Monday before settling near $105.28, and AAA's own Sept 24 release puts the national average at $4.48/gal, the highest ever for this time of year. The weak link is the midterms-strikes claim: it rests solely on the WSJ citing unnamed U.S. officials, and Reuters explicitly said it 'could not immediately confirm the report'; the Post attributes it in the body ('reportedly') but states it unhedged in the headline, and it sits in tension with Trump's public statement, noted in the same article, that he expected the war to end after the midterms. Because the verifiable core is directly confirmed while one headline-level element is only anonymously sourced and unconfirmed, the story is mostly accurate rather than fully accurate.

headline: Donald Trump threat risks fuel rationing as Government confirms who gets first priority
trending_context: Record UK diesel prices; Politico Europe reported a U.S. diesel-export ban under discussion; heavy pickup in UK outlets on September 29.
trending_claim: Trump backed proposals to stop U.S. diesel exports as UK diesel prices hit a record high, prompting UK fuel-rationing contingency planning.
rating_explained: LADbible asserts Trump supports proposals to stop U.S. diesel exports, that UK diesel hit a record, and that emergency fuel plans are in play. The Times reports Trump confirmed Sunday he was considering an all-out diesel export ban ("We're looking at it very seriously — we may do it" to Fox News), and Business Motoring confirms Trump said September 23 he would support proposals to stop diesel exports, with Politico reporting a 90-day export ban under consideration and Energy Secretary Chris Wright pursuing voluntary refiner curbs. BBC reporting (via People Daily) confirms UK diesel hit a new high — 199.33p per liter per the RAC, beating the 199.09p record from June 2022 — and quotes Chancellor John Healey confirming the UK is in talks with the U.S. and "making the provision that we may need to" for a ban. However, the fuel-rationing apparatus cited (emergency powers under the Energy Act 1976, priority access for emergency services and public transport) is pre-existing standing policy, not newly created, so "prompting fuel-rationing contingency planning" slightly overstates causation. Also, LADbible attributes ministerial comments to "Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds" while the BBC attributes the relevant remarks to Chancellor Healey — a minor attribution discrepancy that doesn't affect the core claim. Mostly-accurate.

headline: Ex-White House election official leaves DOJ probe of Trump foes, sources say
trending_context: Major wire story with same-day broad syndication and fresh Google News surfacing.
trending_claim: Kurt Olsen, the second DOJ lawyer on the Florida 'grand conspiracy' probe of Trump's foes, has left the inquiry following Joseph diGenova's resignation.
rating_explained: Reuters reported on September 28, 2026 that Kurt Olsen decided to leave the Florida-based investigation, citing two sources familiar with the matter, while a third source said Olsen remains employed by DOJ. The Associated Press independently confirmed Olsen's resignation from the probe the same day via its own anonymous source, and noted Olsen led a call earlier in September with lawyers for former CIA Director John Brennan, who was informed he is a target. USA Today independently confirmed the other pillar of the claim — that Joseph diGenova resigned from the inquiry on September 10. However, no official DOJ statement confirms Olsen's departure, and the claim rests on anonymous sourcing rather than direct evidence. Given four major outlets (Reuters, AP, CBS, Washington Post) independently report the departure with no denial, the claim is mostly-accurate, but under the direct-evidence standard it cannot be rated fully accurate.

headline: Trump Wanted to Force Postal Workers to Conduct Identity Checks on Mail-in Voters
trending_context: Published September 29; aggregated across tech and political news the same day.
trending_claim: ProPublica found the White House initially wanted postal workers to require mail-in ballots be sent by certified mail — effectively ID checks — and the final March 2026 executive order kept provisions making postal workers vet ballots.
rating_explained: ProPublica's September 28, 2026 investigation reports that the administration initially floated requiring all ballots be delivered exclusively by certified mail, based on several people knowledgeable about the discussions, and that the idea was abandoned after Postal Service objections. ProPublica also confirms the final March 2026 executive order required states to provide voter lists for postal workers to match against ballots, with entire batch mailings rejected over single mismatches. The 'ID check' framing is Gizmodo's extrapolation: certified mail requires the addressee's signature and ID presentation, which ProPublica itself did not characterize as an ID-check scheme. White House spokesperson Lauren Bis denied the certified-mail plan was unworkable and said officials went 'in another direction.' The underlying proposals and final-order vetting provisions are confirmed, so the story is mostly-accurate, with the ID-check label being the outlet's characterization.

headline: Trump Goes Nuclear On Maria Salazar
trending_context: Saturday repost spree after Trump said Salazar and fellow GOP Cuban-Americans should face consequences for opposing his Cuba policy; Politico's original account widely shared.
trending_claim: On Saturday, September 26, 2026, Trump reposted more than a dozen Truth Social messages criticizing Rep. Maria Elvira Salazar, including calls to replace her.
rating_explained: The Crooks and Liars story, quoting Politico, asserts Trump "reposted more than a dozen messages criticizing Salazar on Truth Social," including one reading "So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar." CNN independently reported that Trump "shared in quick succession on Truth Social at least 14 posts from other users critical of Salazar" on Saturday evening, quoting the "nothing but a back stabber" post and the "So we need a NEW Republican to Replace Salazar" post, and obtained a White House official's comment on the posts. Morning Honey independently reports Trump "shared at least 14 posts targeting the Florida congresswoman on Truth Social" on Saturday, with the same quotes and the White House response. The repost count (14), the Saturday timing, and the replacement-call content match across CNN, Politico (via C&L), and Morning Honey. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump Urges Zelenskyy to Settle as Drones Hit Kyiv Again
trending_context: Remarks after his UNGA-week meeting with Zelenskyy; widely covered as Russia hit Kyiv for a third straight night.
trending_claim: On Saturday, September 26, 2026, Trump said he wants Zelenskyy to "settle with Putin" before winter, saying "I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him."
rating_explained: RL News asserts Trump said Saturday he wants Zelenskyy to "settle with Putin." CNN confirms the verbatim quote from Trump's Saturday answer to its question: "But you know what I want him to do? Make a deal. I want him to settle with Putin, and I want Putin to settle with him." EuropeSays confirms the same quote in context: asked about the Patriot-manufacturing-license agreement on September 26, "Trump said he wanted Zelenskyy and Russian President Vladimir Putin to 'settle' their war," following their September 22 UNGA meeting. RL News also reports the drone-strike context — Ukraine's air force said Russia launched 170 drones overnight into Sunday with hits at 18 sites — and EuropeSays confirms strikes killed at least four overnight into September 27, including one person in Kyiv. The central quote is confirmed word-for-word by CNN's direct reporting. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump Shows Xi Biden Autopen Portrait, Gets Criticism Online
trending_context: The White House video of the moment went viral; HuffPost originated the coverage.
trending_claim: During the White House tour with Xi Jinping (the September 24 state visit; the White House shared the video on September 27), Trump pointed to the autopen image replacing Joe Biden's portrait, saying "And this is the autopen. It's Biden."
rating_explained: Mandatory asserts Trump pointed out the autopen image replacing Biden's portrait to Xi, saying "And this is the autopen. It's Biden," captured in the White House's own video. The New York Post confirms: "Xi was filmed laughing as Trump showed off a faux photo depicting former President Joe Biden as an autopen" during the Thursday White House visit. 7Globe, with a Reuters photo, confirms the exchange at the Presidential Walk of Fame: "And, this is the autopen," Trump said, prompting Xi to laugh; "It's Biden," Trump added, tapping Xi on the arm — and that the White House posted the video on social media. Mandatory also confirms the criticism from former Rep. John Delaney ("the most un-American thing an American president has ever done") and ex-deputy press secretary Sarah Matthews, corroborated by 7Globe. The moment, the quote, the White House video, and the criticism are all confirmed by independent outlets. Note: the visit itself was September 24, not September 26 — the White House posted the clip September 27. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump raises eyebrows as he claims US has 'best poverty numbers'
trending_context: The clip went viral on X/Twitter September 28–29; follow-up fact-checks published September 29.
trending_claim: On Sunday, Sept 27, 2026, outside the White House before traveling to the Presidents Cup, Trump told reporters: 'We have the best poverty numbers ever in the history of our country... there's less poverty now than at any time in the history of our country.' Census Bureau data released Sept 15 put the 2025 official poverty rate at a record-low 10.2%, though experts caution the 2025 figures don't reflect 2026 cuts to Medicaid and food assistance, and the supplemental poverty measure was unchanged at 13.1%.
rating_explained: The indy100 story asserts Trump made the remark on Sept 27 and that Census data released earlier this month backs the record-low claim, while noting expert caveats about 2026 policy cuts. Direct evidence confirms all of it: video of Trump's remarks circulated and was transcribed identically by multiple outlets (Primetimer quotes the full statement verbatim), and the Census Bureau's Sept 15, 2026 press release states the official poverty rate fell 0.5 percentage points to 10.2% in 2025. Reuters, reporting the same day, called it 'the lowest on record' and 'the lowest level since the bureau began tracking the measure,' noting the supplemental poverty measure was unchanged at 13.1%. The underlying claim — that the official U.S. poverty rate is the lowest ever recorded — is directly confirmed by the Census Bureau's own data, and the caveats indy100 itself includes (2026 Medicaid/food-assistance cuts, flat SPM) are accurately reported and do not contradict the record-low fact. No major fact-checker has rated this specific claim yet; the verdict rests on the primary source and wire reporting. Verdict: accurate.

sources.name: U.S. Census Bureau — Income, Poverty and Health Insurance Coverage in the United States: 2025 (press release, Sept 15, 2026)
Reuters (via LA Post) — 'US poverty rate dips to lowest on record, Census Bureau says' (Sept 15, 2026)

headline: Poor, Pitiful Donald Trump Caught On Hot Mic Saying He Wants To Go Home
trending_context: The clip went viral on X after the September 27 Presidents Cup at Medinah; picked up by Raw Story and other outlets.
trending_claim: On Sunday, September 27, 2026, a hot mic at the Presidents Cup trophy presentation at Medinah caught Trump saying "I'd like to go home" after shaking hands with U.S. team captain Brandt Snedeker.
rating_explained: The Crooks and Liars story asserts a hot mic caught Trump saying "I'd like to go home" to his staff after shaking Snedeker's hand at the September 27 Presidents Cup. Morning Honey, citing the Daily Beast, reports the president "reportedly said, 'I'd like to go home'" after turning from the players, and embeds the viral September 27 clip posted by the X account Donk Media. Bored Panda independently describes the same sequence: after Trump told Snedeker "You're going to go down in history," he "seemed to say" to those around him, "I'd like to go home." The White House Press Pool's X account corroborates the trophy-presentation timeline that evening (reporters assembled 5:15 p.m., Trump departing for his motorcade within 40 minutes). The claim concerns an audible utterance in a widely circulated video clip; multiple independent outlets report hearing the same words, which is the strongest verification available short of a transcript. C&L itself hedges with "appears to tell his staff," honestly reflecting the clip's background noise. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump uses taxpayer funds for another TV ad, warns of 'final battle'
trending_context: Three such taxpayer-funded ads aired nationally (SNL, NFL games, political shows); bipartisan criticism; covered by Reuters, AP, CNBC, Common Dreams.
trending_claim: A taxpayer-funded TV ad aired during September 27 NFL games that largely mirrors Trump's 2024 campaign ad and frames the midterms as a "final battle."
rating_explained: USA Today asserts a taxpayer-funded ad aired during NFL games on Sunday, September 27, warned of a "final battle," and mirrors a 2024 campaign commercial. Reuters confirms three nationally broadcast ads ending with the disclaimer "Paid for by the US Government," that the "final battle" spot is "nearly identical to one of Trump's campaign spots from 2024," and that the ads "appeared during both 'Saturday Night Live' and NFL football games on Sunday." CNN confirms the ad aired during at least two Sunday NFL games (Commanders-Seahawks and Panthers-Browns on Fox), carries the "Paid for by the US Government" chyron, and matches the video Trump posted on Truth Social in January 2024 except for the campaign-logo ending. Both outlets also document the White House's public-service-announcement defense and bipartisan criticism (Senate Majority Leader John Thune: "shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars"; Sen. John Kennedy; Rep. Thomas Massie). Every material element of the claim is confirmed by wire-level reporting. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump announces largest steel plant in American history to be built in Iowa
trending_context: Major Oval Office announcement on September 28; WSJ first reported the exclusive; one of the biggest stories of September 29.
trending_claim: On September 28, 2026, Trump announced that Mesabi Metallics will build a $15 billion steel plant in Iowa's Lee County, which the White House described as the largest in U.S. history, with production targeted for 2030.
rating_explained: The New York Post story asserts Trump announced the Mesabi Metallics Iowa steel plant in the Oval Office on September 28. The Des Moines Register confirms: Trump "announced Monday, Sept. 28, from the Oval Office that Mesabi Metallics is planning to invest $15 billion into building a steel mill in Iowa," with 6,000 construction jobs and 1,750 permanent jobs, steelmaking beginning in 2030, the mill in Lee County per Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks, and the "largest in U.S. history" characterization explicitly attributed to the White House. Iowa Public Radio independently confirms the $15 billion figure, the Lee County location, Mesabi Metallics as the Minnesota-based builder owned by India's Essar Group, and at least 1,700 permanent high-paying jobs. The announcement, dollar figure, company, county, the White House's "largest" description, and the 2030 timeline are all confirmed by independent on-the-ground reporting. Verdict: accurate.

headline: Trump says he did not discuss the possibility of the US selling weapons to China, contradicting his ambassador
trending_context: Ambassador David Perdue made the claim on Fox News Sunday after the Trump–Xi meeting; State Department pushback followed.
trending_claim: Ambassador David Perdue said on Fox News Sunday that Trump asked Xi Jinping whether China wanted to buy U.S. weapons; Trump denied on Monday that any such discussion took place.
rating_explained: The CNN story asserts Perdue told Fox News Sunday that Trump "actually asked President Xi, would he like to buy some, at one point," and that Trump denied it Monday.
